# CHAPTER XV

DARWINISM (1867-1868)

Politics, diplomacy, law, art, and history had opened no outlet for future energy, but a man must do something in Portland Place when winter evenings are long. Darwin was convulsing society, and Sir Charles Lyell, his geological champion, was intimate at the Legation. Adams was a Darwinist before the letter, a predestined follower of the tide. The atomic theory, the conservation of energy, the kinetic theory of gases, the Law of Natural Selection — these a young man had to take on trust. He was Darwinist because it was easier than not, for his ignorance exceeded belief.

He never tried to understand Darwin; he fancied he might get the best of Darwinism from the easier study of geology. Lyell's new Principles (1866) carried the doctrine through Natural Selection to Natural Evolution, and at last to Natural Uniformity — the very best substitute for religion: a safe, conservative, practical, thoroughly Common-Law deity. Such a system suited a young man who had just helped to waste five or ten thousand million dollars and a million lives to enforce unity on people who objected to it. Unity and Uniformity were the whole motive of philosophy; the best way of reaching unity was to unite, and any road was good that arrived. One had been, from the first, dragged hither and thither like a French poodle on a string, following always the strongest pull.

When Sir Charles came to ask about getting his Principles noticed in America, Adams found nothing simpler than to do it himself — chiefly to educate not the geologists but himself. He struck at once on the Glacial Theory: if the glacial period were uniformity, what was catastrophe? He hinted his heresies in vain; an inserted sentence intended to provoke correction stood unchallenged. Pressed for the simplest case of uniformity, Sir Charles offered *Terebratula*, identical from the beginning of geological time to the end — too much uniformity, too little selection. Asked for the first vertebrate, Sir Charles informed him it was a respectable fish whose bones reposed under Adams's own favorite Abbey on Wenlock Edge.

By 1867 Adams knew Shropshire familiarly, and never tired of rambling over the Edge on a summer afternoon, looking across the Marches to the mountains of Wales. The peculiar flavor of the scenery had to do with absence of evolution; one's instinct abhors time. The Roman road was twin to the railroad; the shepherds of Caractacus would have seen little to surprise them in the modern landscape. But the triumph was to look south along the Edge to the abode of one's earliest ancestor, the ganoid fish *Pteraspis*, whose kingdom was called Siluria. Life began and ended there. Behind that horizon lay only the Cambrian; on the further verge rose the crystalline rocks from which every trace of organic existence had been erased.

Out of his Wenlock musings on Pteraspis Adams carried forward only the suspicion that evolution offered no proof of progress, and that the unity science promised was, like religion, a working hypothesis a historian should accept on faith or not at all.
